blocks.text: K. considered whether he ought not to withdraw in all haste right now; if he did not do so now, there was no prospect that he could do so during the sermon, he would have to stay then for as long as it lasted, at the office he was losing so much time, he had long ceased to be under any obligation to wait for the Italian, he looked at his watch, it was eleven. Yet could a sermon really be preached? Could K. alone represent the congregation? What if he had been a stranger who merely wanted to view the church? At bottom he too was nothing else. It was absurd to think that a sermon was to be preached, now at eleven o'clock, on a weekday in the foulest weather. The priest—a priest he undoubtedly was, a young man with a smooth, dark face—was evidently only going up to put out the lamp that had been lit by mistake.

Yet it was not so, the priest rather examined the light and turned it up a little higher still, then he turned slowly toward the parapet, which he grasped in front by its angular rim with both hands. Thus he stood for a while and looked around without moving his head. K. had retreated a long way and was leaning on his elbows against the foremost pew. With uncertain eyes he saw somewhere, without determining the exact spot, the verger with bent back crouching down peacefully as though after a completed task. What a stillness reigned now in the cathedral! Yet K. had to disturb it, he had no intention of remaining here; if it was the priest's duty to preach at a fixed hour without regard to the circumstances, let him do so, it would succeed even without K.'s assistance, just as K.'s presence would certainly not heighten the effect. Slowly, therefore, K. set himself in motion, felt his way on tiptoe along the pew, came out then into the broad central aisle and walked along there too quite undisturbed, except that the stone floor rang out beneath the lightest step and the vaulting echoed with it faintly, yet continuously, in manifold, regular progression. K. felt a little forsaken as he walked alone there among the empty pews, observed perhaps by the priest, and the size of the cathedral seemed to him, too, to lie just on the borderline of what was still bearable for human beings. When he came to his former place, without pausing further he fairly snatched at the album left lying there and took possession of it. He had almost left the area of the pews and was approaching the open space that lay between them and the exit when for the first time he heard the priest's voice. A powerful, practiced voice. How it penetrated the cathedral ready to receive it! Yet it was not the congregation that the priest called upon, it was quite unmistakable and there were no evasions, he called out: Josef K.!

K. stopped short and looked down at the floor before him. For the moment he was still free, he could still walk on and slip away through one of the three small, dark wooden doors that lay not far ahead of him. It would simply mean that he had not understood, or that he had indeed understood, but did not wish to trouble himself about it. If he turned around, however, he was caught fast, for then he would have made the admission that he had understood quite well, that he really was the one called upon, and that he also meant to obey. Had the priest called out once more, K. would certainly have gone away, but since all remained silent, however long K. waited, he did turn his head a little, for he wanted to see what the priest was doing now. He stood calmly in the pulpit as before, yet it was plain to see that he had noticed the turn of K.'s head. It would have been a childish game of hide-and-seek had K. not turned around completely now. He did so and was beckoned closer by the priest with a crook of his finger. Since everything could now be done openly, he ran—he did so out of curiosity as well and to cut the matter short—with long, flying strides toward the pulpit. At the front pews he came to a halt, but to the priest the distance still seemed too great, he stretched out his hand and pointed with a sharply lowered forefinger to a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed in this too, at this spot he already had to bend his head far back in order still to see the priest. "You are Josef K.," said the priest, raising one hand on the parapet in an indeterminate gesture. "Yes," said K., he thought of how openly he had always given his name in the past, for some time now it had been a burden to him, moreover people whom he was meeting for the first time now knew his name; how fine it was to introduce oneself first and only then to be known. "You are accused," said the priest particularly softly. "Yes," said K., "I have been informed of it." "Then you are the man I am looking for," said the priest. "I am the prison chaplain." "Oh, I see," said K. "I had you summoned here," said the priest, "in order to speak with you." "I did not know that," said K. "I came here to show an Italian the cathedral." "Leave incidental matters aside," said the priest. "What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," answered K., "it is an album of the sights of the city." "Put it down," said the priest. K. flung it away so violently that it flew open and dragged some distance across the floor with crumpled pages. "Do you know that your case is going badly?" asked the priest. "It seems so to me too," said K. "I have made every effort, though thus far without success. To be sure, I have not yet finished the petition." "How do you imagine the end," asked the priest. "Formerly I thought it was bound to end well," said K., "now I sometimes doubt it myself. I do not know how it will end. Do you know?" "No," said the priest, "but I fear it will end badly. You are held to be guilty. Your case will perhaps not even get beyond a lower court. Your guilt is held, provisionally at least, to have been proved." "But I am not guilty," said K. "It is a mistake. How can a human being ever be guilty at all. After all, we are all human beings here, one like another." "That is true," said the priest, "but that is how the guilty are wont to talk." "Do you too have a prejudice against me?" asked K. "I have no prejudice against you," said the priest. "I thank you," said K. "All the others, however, who are involved in the proceedings have a prejudice against me. They instill it into the uninvolved as well. My position grows more and more difficult." "You misunderstand the facts," said the priest. "The verdict does not come all at once, the proceedings gradually merge into the verdict." "So that is how it is," said K., bowing his head. "What do you intend to do next in your case?" asked the priest. "I mean to seek further help," said K. and raised his head to see how the priest would judge this. "There are still certain possibilities that I have not made use of." "You seek too much outside help," said the priest disapprovingly, "and especially from women. Do you really not notice that it is not the true help." "Sometimes and indeed often I could agree with you," said K., "but not always. Women possess great power. If I could induce a few women whom I know to work jointly on my behalf, I would be bound to win through. Especially before this court, which consists almost entirely of womanizers. Show the examining magistrate a woman from afar and he bowls over the court table and the accused, if only to get there in time." The priest bowed his head toward the parapet, only now did the canopy of the pulpit seem to press him down. What sort of storm might there be outside? This was no longer a gloomy day, this was already deep night. No stained glass in the great windows was able to break the dark wall with even a single glimmer. And at this very moment the verger began putting out the candles on the high altar one after another. "Are you angry with me," K. asked the priest. "Perhaps you do not know what sort of court you serve." He received no answer. "After all, those are only my experiences," said K. Up above, all still remained silent. "I did not mean to offend you," said K. Then the priest shouted down to K.: "Can you really not see two paces ahead?" It was shouted in anger, yet at the same time as if by one who sees someone fall and, because he himself is startled, shouts unguardedly, without willing it.
